why: The modern (quantum) description of light is that it travels as **photons obeying the rules of waves** — light carries energy in discrete quanta, yet the probability of finding those quanta is governed by a wave. Each of the other three is an older, superseded or incomplete picture: a *ray* is only a geometrical construction (the path along which energy travels) and has no physical existence of its own; a pure *wave* description is Huygens' and Maxwell's picture, which explains interference and diffraction but fails completely for the photoelectric effect; *corpuscles* is Newton's picture, which fails for interference and diffraction. Only the last option keeps both halves of the dual behaviour.

For a lens optically denser than its surroundings, a positive focal length means a converging lens, and a lens converges when it is thicker at its centre than at its rim. In P the two curved surfaces meet at sharp tips at the top and the bottom, so the rim thickness is zero while the middle is thick — it is a converging meniscus. Q is P mirrored about a vertical line; mirroring swaps the two surfaces and reverses both signs, so \( \dfrac{1}{f} = (n-1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}}\right) \) is unchanged and Q converges too. In R the top and bottom edges are flat and thick while the second surface curves inwards so that the two surfaces almost touch at the middle — thinner at the centre, so R diverges — and S, being R mirrored, diverges as well. Hence exactly **P and Q** have positive focal length. *Only P* is wrong because it forgets that a mirror image of a lens has the same focal length; *Only P and R* and *Only Q and S* each pair one thick-centred lens with one thin-centred one.

Using the chapter's Table 9.1 rule, \( n = \dfrac{360}{\theta} = \dfrac{360}{40} = 9 \), which is an **odd integer**. For an odd integer \( n \) the count depends on where the object sits: on the angle bisector \( N = n - 1 = 8 \), and off the bisector \( N = n = 9 \). The question does not fix the position of the object, so both are possible and the answer is **8 or 9**. *Only 8* and *Only 9* each assert one placement the question never specifies; *9 or 10* is impossible because \( N \) can never exceed \( n = 9 \) (the rule \( N = n \) is the largest case).

\( R = 40\ \text{cm} \Rightarrow f = -20\ \text{cm} \) for a concave mirror. With \( m = -\dfrac{v}{u} \) and \( \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} \), a magnitude of 2 is reached at two places: \( m = +2 \) gives \( u = -10\ \text{cm} \), \( v = +20\ \text{cm} \) — an **erect, virtual** image behind the mirror; \( m = -2 \) gives \( u = -30\ \text{cm} \), \( v = -60\ \text{cm} \) — a real, inverted image formed 60 cm in *front* of the mirror. A shaving mirror must show the face the right way up and must not form its image in mid-air in front of the glass, so only the erect virtual case is usable and the object distance is **10 cm only**. *20 cm only* is the focus, where no image is formed at all; *30 cm only* gives the inverted real image; *10 cm or 30 cm* is the answer if the words 'used for shaving purpose' are ignored, and it is that phrase which selects the erect image.

**Chromatic aberration** is caused by the refractive index of a material varying with colour, so that different colours are brought to different foci. Reflection at a mirror involves no refractive index at all: the law of reflection \( i = r \) is the same for every wavelength, so a mirror focuses all colours identically and chromatic aberration cannot arise. The other three do occur for spherical mirrors — *spherical aberration* arises from the spherical shape of the reflecting surface itself (marginal rays focus nearer the pole than paraxial rays), and *coma* and *distortion* arise, as the chapter states, from beams of rays inclined to the principal axis.

Let \( h \) be the common value of the tree height and the fish's depth. The fish looks up at an object in air, so the apparent height is *magnified*: \( n\,h = 2.5 \). The monkey looks down at an object in water, so the apparent depth is *reduced*: \( \dfrac{h}{n} = 1.6 \). Multiplying the two removes \( n \): \( h^{2} = 2.5 \times 1.6 = 4 \), so \( h = 2\ \text{m} \) and \( n = \dfrac{2.5}{2} = \dfrac{5}{4} \). Checking the other three against the second condition: \( n = 6/5 \) gives \( h = 2.083 \) and an apparent depth of 1.74 m; \( n = 4/3 \) gives 1.41 m; \( n = 7/5 \) gives 1.28 m. None of these is the required 1.6 m, so **5/4** is the only consistent value.

This chapter rules out two of the four by name. For the **rainbow** it says the ray 'internally (NOT total internally) reflects' inside the drop, and lists as a fact that 'total internal reflection is not possible in this case' — the internal reflection there is only partial, which is why the emerging rainbow is faint. For the **mirage** it says that total internal reflection 'is NEVER possible here, because the relative refractive index is just less than 1 and hence the critical angle is also approaching \( 90^\circ \)'; the upward bending comes from a very large reflection coefficient at grazing incidence, not from TIR. That leaves the **optical fibre**, in which the signal survives kilometres precisely by repeated total internal reflection at the core–cladding boundary, and the **glittering of a diamond**, whose very high refractive index gives a critical angle of about \( 24^\circ \) so that light entering is totally internally reflected many times before it escapes. Hence total internal reflection is involved only in the optical fibre and in the glittering of a diamond.

The 'number' of a spectacle lens is its focal power in dioptre, so \( P = -2\ \text{D} \) means \( f = -0.5\ \text{m} \): a **diverging** lens, as is required to correct short sight (myopia) for distant objects. The chapter states which shape is actually ground for this: 'concavo-convex and convexo-concave lenses are commonly used for spectacles of positive and negative numbers, respectively.' A negative number therefore takes the **convexo-concave** meniscus. *Bi-concave* and *double concave* are two names for the same shape, so neither could be a unique answer, and in any case a double-concave blank is not what is ground for spectacles; *concavo-convex* is the shape used for a positive number.

The bubble sits at the **centre** of the sphere, so every ray leaving it travels along a radius and therefore meets the spherical surface exactly along the normal. A ray incident along the normal passes out undeviated, so the emergent rays still diverge from the centre and the bubble is seen exactly where it is. The formula agrees: with \( n_{1} = 1.5 \), \( n_{2} = 1 \), \( u = -1.5\ \text{cm} \) and \( R = -1.5\ \text{cm} \), \( \dfrac{n_{2} - n_{1}}{R} = \dfrac{n_{2}}{v} - \dfrac{n_{1}}{u} \) gives \( \dfrac{-0.5}{-1.5} = \dfrac{1}{v} + 1 \), so \( v = -1.5\ \text{cm} \) — one full radius inside the surface, i.e. **at the centre**. The distances 1 cm, 5/3 cm and 2 cm are all different from the 1.5 cm radius, so none of them places the image at the centre.

Angular dispersion for a thin prism is \( \delta_{VR} = A(n_{V} - n_{R}) \), which is **directly** proportional to the refracting angle \( A \). So a *larger* prism angle, not a smaller one, gives greater angular dispersion; the statement recommending a smaller angle of prism for greater angular dispersion is the wrong one. The other three are correct: a right-angled isosceles glass prism is the standard total-internal-reflection element in binoculars and periscopes, since its \( 45^\circ \) internal incidence exceeds the critical angle of about \( 42^\circ \) for glass; for a thin prism \( \delta = A(n-1) \) contains no \( i \) at all, so the deviation is practically constant; and because \( r_{1} + r_{2} = A \), the emergent ray exists only while \( r_{2} \) stays below the critical angle, which forces \( r_{1} \) — and hence \( i \) — to exceed a certain minimum.

Dispersive power is the ratio of angular dispersion to mean deviation, \( \omega = \dfrac{\delta_{V} - \delta_{R}}{\left( \dfrac{\delta_{V} + \delta_{R}}{2} \right)} = \dfrac{2(\delta_{V} - \delta_{R})}{\delta_{V} + \delta_{R}} \). Evaluating each pair: \( 7^\circ, 10^\circ \Rightarrow \dfrac{2 \times 3}{17} = 0.353 \); \( 8^\circ, 11^\circ \Rightarrow \dfrac{2 \times 3}{19} = 0.316 \); \( 12^\circ, 16^\circ \Rightarrow \dfrac{2 \times 4}{28} = 0.286 \); \( 10^\circ, 14^\circ \Rightarrow \dfrac{2 \times 4}{24} = 0.333 \). The largest is 0.353, for the pair \( 7^\circ \) and \( 10^\circ \). Note that the biggest *difference* (4°) belongs to two other pairs — it is the difference divided by the mean that matters, and the small mean deviation of the first pair is what wins.

In a rainbow, sunlight refracts on entering the water drop, reflects once (primary) or twice (secondary) at the inner surface, and refracts again on leaving; the different colours emerge along different directions, giving angular dispersion, and each colour is turned through its own angular deviation. The chapter is explicit that the inner reflection is 'internally (NOT total internally) reflect' and states as fact that 'total internal reflection is not possible in this case' — light must be able to *leave* the drop for the bow to be seen at all, which a total internal reflection would forbid. So **total internal reflection** is the one process not involved; refraction, angular dispersion and angular deviation all are.

Statement (R) is correct — the chapter says of a magnifying glass that 'convex lens used for this purpose is a simple microscope'. Statement (P) is correct too: without an instrument the object cannot be brought closer than the least distance of distinct vision \( D \), whereas a simple microscope lets the object be placed within its focus, i.e. inside \( D \), while the image it forms stays at or beyond \( D \). Statement (Q) is **wrong**: from the limiting cases, an object at the focus sends the image to infinity and gives \( M_{min} = \dfrac{D}{f} \), the *smallest* magnifying power; the largest, \( M_{max} = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f} \), is obtained when the object is brought closer still so that the image forms at \( D \). Hence only (P) and (R) are correct. Every option containing (Q) is excluded by that limiting-case result, and the option naming (P) alone drops the correct statement (R).
